message.content: In probability theory, one might ask whether it is possible for two discrete random variables X and Y to have finite expectations while the expectation of their sum is undefined or infinite. The answer to this question is yes, such examples do exist. The key insight lies in understanding how the expectation of a sum relates to the individual expectations. When both E(X) and E(Y) exist and are finite, one might naively expect that E(X + Y) must also be finite. However, this is not necessarily true in the context of discrete random variables. The issue arises when the positive and negative parts of X + Y both have infinite expectations. Recall that for a discrete random variable Z, E(Z) is defined only when at least one of E(Z⁺) or E(Z⁻) is finite. If both E(Z⁺) and E(Z⁻) are infinite, then E(Z) is undefined. To construct such an example, we need to be careful about how X and Y are defined. One approach is to define X and Y on the same probability space with specific distributions. Let us consider a probability space with outcomes indexed by the positive integers. We can assign probabilities to these outcomes in a way that makes both E(X) and E(Y) finite. However, the sum X + Y may behave differently at the tails of the distribution. Specifically, we can arrange for the positive part of X + Y to have infinite expectation. Similarly, we can arrange for the negative part of X + Y to also have infinite expectation. This ensures that E(X + Y) is undefined, even though E(X) and E(Y) are both finite. The construction relies on the fact that X and Y can have cancelling terms that do not appear in their individual expectations. Each of X and Y individually has a well-behaved tail that ensures finite expectation. But when we add them together, the tails can produce a distribution with divergent positive and negative parts. This phenomenon is a subtlety that often surprises students of probability theory. It highlights the importance of understanding the precise conditions under which linearity of expectation holds. The linearity property E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) requires that the expectations involved are well-defined. It is worth noting that this particular subtlety in the theory of expectation for discrete random variables is one that many students and even some experienced instructors tend to overlook or dismiss as beneath the surface of standard textbook treatments of the subject.
